rows.stem: The electric field (E) and electric potential (V) at a point inside a charged hollow metallic sphere are respectively :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(E = 0\) and \(V = V_0\), a non-zero constant.**

**The field inside is ZERO.** Take any Gaussian surface inside the cavity of the hollow conductor. It encloses no charge — all the charge resides on the **outer surface** of the metal — so the flux through it vanishes, and by symmetry so does \(\vec{E}\) at every interior point.

\(\boxed{\ E = 0\ \text{everywhere inside}\ }\)

**But the POTENTIAL is not zero.** The two are related by

\(E = -\dfrac{dV}{dr}\)

so \(E = 0\) says only that \(V\) does not **change** — it is **constant**, not that it is zero. A vanishing gradient means a flat function, and a flat function need not sit at zero.

\(\boxed{\ V = V_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{Q}{R}\ \text{throughout the interior}\ }\)

where \(R\) is the sphere's radius. **The interior is at the SAME potential as the surface**, because no work is needed to carry a charge from the surface to any interior point against a zero field.

**Option (A) is the trap, and it is a confusion of two different quantities.** Zero field does not imply zero potential any more than a flat road implies sea level. The two would coincide only if the sphere were uncharged, or earthed.

**A picture of the whole thing.** Plotting \(V\) against distance from the centre: it is **flat** at \(V_0\) from the centre out to the surface, and then falls as \(1/r\) outside, like a point charge \(Q\) at the centre. \(E\) is correspondingly **zero** inside, jumps to \(Q/4\pi\varepsilon_0R^{2}\) at the surface, and falls as \(1/r^{2}\) beyond — a discontinuity in \(E\) at a surface charge, but \(V\) itself stays continuous.

**Why the charge sits on the outside.** Like charges repel, so they spread as far apart as they can get — which on a conductor means the outer surface. Inside the metal itself the field must be zero in equilibrium, or the free electrons would still be moving.

**This is electrostatic shielding**, and it is why a sensitive instrument is placed inside a metal enclosure and why a car body protects its occupants from lightning. Note that it protects against **external** fields only: a charge placed inside the cavity would produce a field there that nothing screens.

rows.subtopic: Biot-Savart Law and Field of a Circular Loop
rows.stem: In a circular loop of radius R, current I enters at point A and exits at point B, as shown in the figure. The value of the magnetic field at the centre O of the loop is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names the points A, B and O but says nothing about where they sit on the loop, so the geometry exists only in the drawing. What is drawn: a single circle with its centre marked O; a point A on the circle at the left end of the horizontal radius, reached by a straight lead carrying an arrow labelled I that points towards the loop; a point B on the circle at the top of the vertical radius, with a straight lead leaving upward under an arrow. The two radii OA and OB are drawn dashed and carry a right-angle mark at O. DESCRIBED: the labelling and the layout. WITHHELD: the resulting field at O, which is what the four options offer. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): zero.**

**The current splits into two arcs**, which are two resistors in **parallel** between the entry point \(A\) and the exit point \(B\). The field at the centre is the sum of their two contributions, and the striking result is that they cancel **exactly**.

**Step 1 — how the current divides.** Each arc's resistance is proportional to its length, hence to the angle it subtends at the centre:

\(R_1 \propto \theta_1, \qquad R_2 \propto \theta_2\)

Being in parallel, they carry the same potential difference:

\(i_1R_1 = i_2R_2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad i_1\theta_1 = i_2\theta_2\)

**Step 2 — the field each arc produces at the centre.** For an arc of angle \(\theta\) carrying current \(i\) at radius \(R\):

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i\theta}{4\pi R}\)

So

\(B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i_1\theta_1}{4\pi R}, \qquad B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i_2\theta_2}{4\pi R}\)

**Step 3 — and \(i\theta\) is the same for both, by Step 1:**

\(B_1 = B_2\)

**Step 4 — the directions are OPPOSITE.** Travelling from \(A\) to \(B\), one arc goes clockwise round the centre and the other anticlockwise, so by the right-hand rule one field points out of the plane and the other into it.

\(\boxed{\ B_{\text{net}} = B_1 - B_2 = 0\ }\)

**Why this holds for ANY positions of A and B** — and that is the whole point of the question. The **same product \(i\theta\)** governs both the current division and the field, so whatever the split, the two contributions match. A longer arc has proportionally more resistance and so carries proportionally less current, and the two effects cancel identically.

*Here \(A\) and \(B\) happen to be diametrically opposite, so each arc is a semicircle carrying \(I/2\) and producing \(\mu_0I/8R\) — equal and opposite. But the answer would still be zero for any other placement.*

**The distractors are the fields of complete loops or arcs.** \(\mu_0I/2R\) is a full circular loop carrying \(I\); \(\mu_0I/4R\) is a semicircle carrying \(I\). Both would be right if all the current went round one way — which is exactly what does **not** happen when the loop is fed at two points.

**A neat way to remember it.** The arrangement is a **balanced** divider by construction: resistance and arc angle are the same quantity in different units, so the loop always splits the current in precisely the ratio needed to null the field at its centre.

rows.stem: The mass numbers of two nuclei A and B are 27 and 64 respectively. The ratio of their radii \(\left(\dfrac{r_{\mathrm{A}}}{r_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\) will be :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (D): \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).**

**The nuclear radius formula.**

\(R = R_0A^{1/3} \qquad\text{with}\qquad R_0 = 1{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{fm}\)

so

\(\dfrac{r_A}{r_B} = \left(\dfrac{A_A}{A_B}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{27}{64}\right)^{1/3}\)

**Both numbers are perfect cubes**, which is why they were chosen:

\(27 = 3^{3}, \qquad 64 = 4^{3}\)

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{r_A}{r_B} = \dfrac{3}{4}\ }\)

**Each distractor is the wrong power.** Option (A), \(\tfrac{27}{64}\), is the ratio with **no** root taken at all — the first power. Option (B), \(\tfrac{9}{16}\), is \(\left(3/4\right)^{2}\), the ratio of **areas** rather than radii. Option (C), \(\tfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}\), is \(\left(27/64\right)^{1/2}\) — the square root where the **cube** root was wanted.

**Why the cube root, physically.** The volume of a nucleus is found to be proportional to its mass number:

\(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} \propto A\)

**Nuclear matter has essentially CONSTANT DENSITY**, about \(2{\cdot}3 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), the same for every nucleus from helium to uranium. So packing in \(A\) nucleons takes a volume proportional to \(A\), and the radius follows as \(A^{1/3}\).

**That constant density is a real physical result**, not a mathematical convenience, and it follows from the **saturation** of the nuclear force: each nucleon binds only to its immediate neighbours, not to every other nucleon, so adding more simply enlarges the nucleus rather than compressing it. The same saturation is why the binding energy per nucleon stays roughly flat across the periodic table.

**The contrast with an atom.** Atomic radii vary only feebly with \(Z\) — all atoms are within a factor of a few of \(10^{-10}\) m — because electron shells fill outward against an increasing nuclear pull. Nuclear radii, by contrast, follow \(A^{1/3}\) cleanly over the whole range.

**The actual sizes here:** \(r_A = 1{\cdot}2 \times 3 = 3{\cdot}6\) fm and \(r_B = 1{\cdot}2 \times 4 = 4{\cdot}8\) fm. The mass number more than doubles while the radius grows by only a third.

rows.stem: Two wires made of the same material have the same length (\(l\)) but different cross-sectional areas \(\mathrm{A_1}\) and \(\mathrm{A_2}\). They are connected together with a cell of voltage V. Find the ratio of the drift velocities of free electrons in the two wires when they are joined in (i) series, and (ii) parallel.
rows.solution:
**The relation to work from.**

\(I = neAv_d \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v_d = \dfrac{I}{neA}\)

The wires are of the **same material**, so \(n\) and \(e\) are common and cancel from any ratio. Everything then depends on what the connection holds fixed.

**(i) In SERIES — the same CURRENT flows through both.**

With \(I\) common,

\(v_d \propto \dfrac{1}{A}\)

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{v_{d_1}}{v_{d_2}} = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}\ }\)

**The ratio is INVERTED**, which is the point: the thinner wire carries the same number of electrons per second through a smaller opening, so each must move faster. This is why a river speeds up where its channel narrows.

**(ii) In PARALLEL — the same VOLTAGE appears across both.**

Here the current is **not** common, so go back to the field instead:

\(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}\cdot\dfrac{V}{l}\)

**Both wires have the same length \(l\) and the same \(V\) across them**, so both carry the **same electric field** — and the same material gives the same \(\tau\), \(e\) and \(m\).

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{v_{d_1}}{v_{d_2}} = 1 \qquad\text{— the drift velocities are EQUAL}\ }\)

**The areas are irrelevant in parallel**, and that is what the two parts together are testing. Drift velocity is governed by the **field**, and the field in a wire of given length under a given potential difference does not care how thick the wire is. The thicker wire does carry **more current** \(\left(I = neAv_d\right)\) — but by having more electrons in the drift, not by drifting faster.

**The same two conductors give completely different answers** depending only on how they are joined, which is why reading that one word decides the question:

| | Common quantity | \(v_{d_1}/v_{d_2}\) |
|---|---|---|
| **Series** | current \(I\) | \(A_2/A_1\) |
| **Parallel** | voltage \(V\), hence field \(E\) | \(1\) |

**A check on the series case.** In series the thinner wire also has the larger resistance \(\left(R = \rho l/A\right)\) and so drops the larger share of the voltage — a larger field across it, and hence a larger drift velocity. The two routes, current-based and field-based, agree.

**Why "same length" matters for part (ii).** Equal lengths are what make the two fields equal when the voltages are equal. Wires of different lengths in parallel would have \(E = V/l\) differing, and the drift velocities would differ in the inverse ratio of the lengths.

rows.stem: The ratio of the intensities at maxima to minima in Young's double-slit experiment is 25 : 9. Calculate the ratio of intensities of the interfering waves.
rows.solution:
**The intensities at the maxima and minima.**

\(I_{\max} = \left(a_1 + a_2\right)^{2}, \qquad I_{\min} = \left(a_1 - a_2\right)^{2}\)

where \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) are the **amplitudes** of the two interfering waves. Intensity goes as amplitude squared, so the amplitudes add at a maximum and subtract at a minimum.

**Set up the given ratio.**

\(\dfrac{\left(a_1 + a_2\right)^{2}}{\left(a_1 - a_2\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{25}{9}\)

**Take the square root of both sides** — the step that makes the rest linear:

\(\dfrac{a_1 + a_2}{a_1 - a_2} = \dfrac{5}{3}\)

**Cross-multiplying:**

\(3\left(a_1 + a_2\right) = 5\left(a_1 - a_2\right)\)

\(3a_1 + 3a_2 = 5a_1 - 5a_2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 8a_2 = 2a_1\)

\(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{4}{1}\)

**Then square to get back to intensities.**

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{16}{1}\ }\)

**Two squarings and one square-rooting** — that is the whole structure of the problem, and losing track of which stage you are at is the only real hazard. The given \(25 : 9\) is a ratio of **intensities**; \(5 : 3\) is the corresponding ratio of **sums and differences of amplitudes**; \(4 : 1\) is the ratio of **amplitudes**; \(16 : 1\) is back to **intensities**.

**Checking the answer forwards**, which is quick and worth doing. If \(a_1 : a_2 = 4 : 1\), then

\(I_{\max} \propto \left(4 + 1\right)^{2} = 25, \qquad I_{\min} \propto \left(4 - 1\right)^{2} = 9\)

giving \(25 : 9\) as required. \(\checkmark\)

**Why the minima are not dark.** \(I_{\min} = 9\) rather than \(0\), because the amplitudes are **unequal** — a stronger wave cannot be fully cancelled by a weaker one. Perfect darkness at the minima requires \(a_1 = a_2\), and then \(I_{\max}/I_{\min}\) would be infinite. The finite ratio \(25 : 9\) is a direct measure of how poorly matched the two beams are.

**The general relation this illustrates.** With \(r = a_1/a_2\),

\(\dfrac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = \left(\dfrac{r + 1}{r - 1}\right)^{2}\)

so the **contrast** of the fringe pattern is fixed entirely by the amplitude ratio. Making the two slits equally wide is how the ratio is driven towards \(1\) and the fringes made as sharp as possible.

rows.stem:
Calculate the binding energy per nucleon (in MeV) of a helium nucleus \((^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He})\).
Given : \(\mathrm{m}(^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}) = 4{\cdot}002603\) u
\(\mathrm{m_n} = 1{\cdot}008665\) u
\(\mathrm{m_H} = 1{\cdot}007825\) u
\(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931{\cdot}5\) MeV/c\(^2\)
rows.solution:
**The mass defect.** A helium-4 nucleus contains \(2\) protons and \(2\) neutrons:

\(\Delta m = \left[2m_H + 2m_n\right] - m\left({}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\right)\)

**Note that \(m_H\) is the mass of the hydrogen ATOM, not the bare proton**, and \(m\left({}^{4}\mathrm{He}\right)\) is likewise the atomic mass. Using atomic masses on both sides makes the **two electrons on each side cancel exactly**, so the electron masses never have to be handled. That is why the data is given this way, and substituting the proton mass instead would be a small but real error.

**Substituting.**

\(2m_H = 2 \times 1{\cdot}007825 = 2{\cdot}015650\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(2m_n = 2 \times 1{\cdot}008665 = 2{\cdot}017330\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\text{sum} = 4{\cdot}032980\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(\Delta m = 4{\cdot}032980 - 4{\cdot}002603 = 0{\cdot}030377\ \mathrm{u}\)

**The total binding energy.**

\(BE = \Delta m \times 931{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0{\cdot}030377 \times 931{\cdot}5\)

\(BE = 28{\cdot}30\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

**The binding energy per nucleon.**

\(\dfrac{BE}{A} = \dfrac{28{\cdot}30}{4}\)

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{BE}{A} = 7{\cdot}07\ \mathrm{MeV per nucleon}\ }\)

*(The printed scheme writes the conversion factor as \(931\) while the question supplies \(931{\cdot}5\); its stated \(28{\cdot}2962\) MeV corresponds to \(931{\cdot}5\). Either constant gives \(7{\cdot}07\) MeV per nucleon to three figures.)*

**Why the seven-figure masses matter.** \(\Delta m\) is a difference between two numbers agreeing to four significant figures — rounding the inputs even to five places would destroy it. This is the normal situation in nuclear physics and the reason atomic masses are tabulated so finely.

**What the number means.** \(7{\cdot}07\) MeV per nucleon is **exceptionally high for so light a nucleus**. Its neighbours are far below it: \({}^{3}\)H manages \(2{\cdot}83\), \({}^{6}\)Li only \(5{\cdot}33\). Helium-4 sits on a local peak of the binding-energy curve.

**Why \({}^{4}\)He is so tightly bound.** Two protons and two neutrons complete a closed shell of each — a "doubly magic" nucleus — which is why it is so stable and why it is emitted intact in **alpha decay** rather than as separate nucleons. It is also why helium is the end product of hydrogen fusion in stars, and the reason that step releases so much energy.

**A comparison worth carrying.** The peak of the whole curve, near iron, is about \(8{\cdot}8\) MeV per nucleon — so helium-4 already reaches \(80\%\) of the maximum achievable binding with only four nucleons.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
(a) Briefly explain Einstein's photoelectric equation.
(b) Four metals with their work functions are listed below :
K = \(2{\cdot}3\) eV, Na = \(2{\cdot}75\) eV, Mo = \(4{\cdot}17\) eV and Ni = \(5{\cdot}15\) eV.
The radiation of wavelength 330 nm from a laser source placed 1 m away, falls on these metals. Which of these metals will not show photoelectric emission ? What will happen if the laser source is brought closer to a distance of 50 cm ?
rows.solution:
**(a) Einstein's photoelectric equation.**

\(\boxed{\ h\nu = \phi_0 + K_{\max}\ }\)

**What each term is.**

\(h\nu\) — the energy of **one incident photon**, brought by a single quantum of the radiation.

\(\phi_0\) — the **work function**, the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal surface.

\(K_{\max}\) — the **maximum kinetic energy** of an emitted photoelectron, the remainder.

**The physical statement.** A photon is absorbed **entirely by a single electron**, all at once — it cannot be shared and cannot be absorbed in part. Of its energy, \(\phi_0\) is spent escaping the surface; whatever is left appears as kinetic energy. So

\(K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)

**Emission occurs only if \(h\nu \ge \phi_0\)**, which is the threshold condition. Below it \(K_{\max}\) would be negative — impossible — and **no electron is emitted, however intense the light**.

**Why "maximum".** Only electrons escaping from the very surface pay nothing beyond \(\phi_0\); those freed deeper lose energy in collisions on the way out. So the emitted electrons span every energy from zero up to \(K_{\max}\), and the equation fixes the **top** of that range.

**(b) Which metals emit, and what changes when the source is moved.**

**The photon energy at \(330\) nm.**

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{330 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(E = 3{\cdot}77\ \mathrm{eV}\)

*(Or by the shortcut \(hc = 1240\) eV·nm: \(1240/330 = 3{\cdot}76\) eV.)*

**Compare with each work function.**

| Metal | \(\phi_0\) | \(E = 3{\cdot}77\) eV | Emission? |
|---|---|---|---|
| K | \(2{\cdot}30\) eV | \(E > \phi_0\) | **yes**, \(K_{\max} = 1{\cdot}47\) eV |
| Na | \(2{\cdot}75\) eV | \(E > \phi_0\) | **yes**, \(K_{\max} = 1{\cdot}02\) eV |
| Mo | \(4{\cdot}17\) eV | \(E < \phi_0\) | **NO** |
| Ni | \(5{\cdot}15\) eV | \(E < \phi_0\) | **NO** |

\(\boxed{\ \text{Mo and Ni will NOT show photoelectric emission.}\ }\)

**Bringing the source to 50 cm.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{NO CHANGE in which metals emit — Mo and Ni still show nothing.}\ }\)

**Why.** Halving the distance **quadruples the intensity** by the inverse-square law, so **four times as many photons** arrive each second. But the **wavelength is unchanged**, so each photon still carries exactly \(3{\cdot}77\) eV — still below the work functions of Mo and Ni. A photon cannot be topped up by its neighbours; each acts alone on one electron.

**What DOES change, for K and Na.** More photons means more photoelectrons, so the **photocurrent quadruples**. But \(K_{\max}\) depends on \(\nu\) alone and is **unaltered**, so the stopping potential stays exactly where it was.

**This is the whole of the photoelectric effect in one question.** On the wave picture a brighter beam delivers more energy and should eventually free electrons from any metal — yet quadrupling the intensity here does nothing at all for Mo and Ni. **Intensity controls how MANY; frequency controls how ENERGETIC.** Only a shorter wavelength would bring Mo and Ni into play: they would need \(297\) nm and \(241\) nm respectively.

rows.stem:
(a) How are electromagnetic waves produced ?
(b) Write the wavelength range and one use of :
(i) Microwaves, and
(ii) Ultraviolet waves.
rows.solution:
**(a) How electromagnetic waves are produced.**

An electromagnetic wave is produced by an **ACCELERATING electric charge** — in practice, by a charge **oscillating** with some frequency.

**The mechanism, in the order the fields appear.** An oscillating charge constitutes a time-varying current, which sets up a **changing magnetic field** around it. By Faraday's law a changing magnetic field produces a **changing electric field**; and by the Ampere-Maxwell law — through the displacement-current term — that changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field in turn.

**Each field regenerates the other**, so once launched the disturbance sustains itself and propagates outwards, needing no medium and no further help from the source. **The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge.**

**Acceleration is the necessary condition.** A **stationary** charge produces only a static field and radiates nothing. A charge in **uniform motion** constitutes a steady current, giving a steady magnetic field, and radiates nothing either. Only when the motion **changes** does energy detach from the charge and travel away.

*A concrete case:* an LC oscillator feeding an aerial drives charge up and down at the circuit's resonant frequency, radiating radio waves of exactly that frequency.

**(b)(i) Microwaves.**

**Wavelength range:** about \(0{\cdot}1\) m down to \(1\) mm \(\left(10^{-1}\ \text{to}\ 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\right)\).

**One use:** **RADAR** — in aircraft navigation and speed measurement. Microwaves are short enough to be beamed narrowly by a modest antenna and long enough to pass through cloud and rain, which is the combination radar needs.

*(Also: microwave ovens, which work by resonating with the rotational frequency of water molecules; and satellite communication, since microwaves penetrate the ionosphere where radio waves are reflected.)*

**(b)(ii) Ultraviolet waves.**

**Wavelength range:** about \(400\) nm down to \(1\) nm \(\left(4 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{to}\ 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\right)\).

**One use:** **sterilisation** — killing germs in water purifiers and on surgical instruments. UV photons carry a few electronvolts, enough to break the chemical bonds in a microorganism's DNA.

*(Also: LASIK eye surgery, which uses an excimer laser to reshape the cornea; and detecting forged banknotes and signatures by fluorescence.)*

**The single principle behind both uses.** What a band of the spectrum is good for is decided by its **photon energy** \(E = h\nu\), and hence by what it can interact with. Microwave photons carry about \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-3}\) eV — enough to set molecules rotating but far too little to damage them. Ultraviolet photons carry a few eV — enough to break bonds, which is exactly why they sterilise and equally why they are dangerous to skin and eyes.

rows.stem:
(a) Two concentric circular coils of radii \(\mathrm{r_1}\) and \(\mathrm{r_2}\) \((\mathrm{r_2} \gg \mathrm{r})\) are placed coaxially with their centres coinciding. If a current I is passed through the outer coil, obtain the expression for mutual inductance of the arrangement.
(b) The current in a solenoid decreases steadily from 6 mA to 2 mA in 50 ms. If an average emf of \(0{\cdot}4\) V is induced, find the self-inductance of the solenoid.
rows.solution:
**(a) Mutual inductance of two concentric coils.**

**The set-up.** Two coplanar concentric circular coils of radii \(r_1\) and \(r_2\), with \(r_2 \gg r_1\) — a **small** coil at the centre of a **large** one. Current \(I\) is passed through the **outer** coil.

**Step 1 — the field of the outer coil at its centre.**

\(B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r_2}\)

**Step 2 — treat that field as uniform across the inner coil.** This is where \(r_2 \gg r_1\) earns its place: the outer coil's field varies over its own interior, but across the tiny region occupied by the inner coil it is effectively constant at its central value. Without that condition the flux would need integrating and no simple expression would exist.

**Step 3 — the flux linked with the inner coil.**

\(\phi_1 = B_2 \times \pi r_1^{2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r_2}\cdot\pi r_1^{2}\)

**Note it is \(r_1\) in the area, not \(r_2\)** — the area that matters is that of the coil doing the **linking**.

**Step 4 — the mutual inductance**, from \(\phi_1 = MI\):

\(\boxed{\ M = \dfrac{\mu_0\pi r_1^{2}}{2r_2}\ }\)

**Why the current must be passed through the OUTER coil for this to be easy.** Reversing the roles — current in the small coil, flux through the large one — gives a field that is highly non-uniform over the outer coil's area, and the integral is intractable. Yet by **reciprocity** \(M\) is the same either way, so computing the easy case gives the answer to the hard one. That is the standard use of \(M_{12} = M_{21}\): choose whichever direction the symmetry favours.

**(b) The self-inductance of the solenoid.**

\(\left|\varepsilon\right| = L\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right| \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad L = \dfrac{\left|\varepsilon\right|}{\left|dI/dt\right|}\)

**The rate of change of current**, converting both the milliamps and the milliseconds:

\(\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{\left(6 - 2\right) \times 10^{-3}}{50 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-2}} = 0{\cdot}08\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}\)

**Both conversions are needed**, and they partly offset — the \(10^{-3}\) of the milliamps against the \(10^{-3}\) of the milliseconds — which is why the rate comes out as a modest \(0{\cdot}08\) A/s rather than something extreme.

\(L = \dfrac{0{\cdot}4}{0{\cdot}08}\)

\(\boxed{\ L = 5\ \mathrm{H}\ }\)

**A sense of the value.** \(5\) H is a **large** inductance — a coil of many thousands of turns on an iron core, not an air-cored solenoid. It is the sort of choke used in a power supply, and it is what allows a current change of only \(4\) mA to induce as much as \(0{\cdot}4\) V over \(50\) ms.

**Note that "average emf" matches "steadily".** The current falls at a constant rate, so \(dI/dt\) is the same throughout and the induced emf is genuinely steady rather than merely averaged. The two words are consistent, and either alone would have been enough.

rows.subtopic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges
rows.stem:
Two point charges of \(-5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) are located in free space at \((-4\ \mathrm{cm}, 0)\) and \((6\ \mathrm{cm}, 0)\) respectively.
(a) Calculate the amount of work done to separate the two charges at infinite distance.
(b) If this system of charges was initially kept in an electric field \(\mathrm{E} = \dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{r^2}\), where \(\mathrm{A} = 8 \times 10^4\) N C\(^{-1}\) m\(^2\), calculate the electrostatic potential energy of the system.
rows.solution:
**The separation.** The charges sit at \(x = -4\) cm and \(x = +6\) cm, so

\(r = 6 - \left(-4\right) = 10\ \mathrm{cm} = 0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{m}\)

**(a) The work done to separate them to infinity.**

**The initial potential energy of the pair.**

\(U_i = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times \left(-5 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{0{\cdot}1}\)

\(U_i = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times \left(-10^{-11}\right)}{0{\cdot}1} = -0{\cdot}9\ \mathrm{J}\)

**At infinity the energy is zero**, so the work an external agent must do is

\(W = U_f - U_i = 0 - \left(-0{\cdot}9\right)\)

\(\boxed{\ W = +0{\cdot}9\ \mathrm{J}\ }\)

**The positive sign is the physics.** The charges are of **opposite** sign, so they attract; pulling them apart is work done **against** that attraction, and energy must be supplied from outside. Had they been like charges, \(U_i\) would be positive and the separation would release energy instead.

**(b) The energy of the system in the external field.**

**First find the potential of the external field.** Given \(E = A/r^{2}\) and \(E = -dV/dr\):

\(dV = -\dfrac{A}{r^{2}}dr \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad V = \dfrac{A}{r}\)

taking \(V \to 0\) as \(r \to \infty\). *(This is the field of a point charge at the origin, with \(A = q/4\pi\varepsilon_0\).)*

**The total energy now has THREE contributions**, and leaving out the third is the error this part is built to catch:

\(U = q_1V_1 + q_2V_2 + \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r}\)

the first two being each charge's energy in the **external** field, the third their **mutual** interaction — which has not gone away.

**The potentials at the two locations**, using distances from the origin:

\(V_1 = \dfrac{A}{0{\cdot}04} = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{4}}{4 \times 10^{-2}} = 2 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(V_2 = \dfrac{A}{0{\cdot}06} = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{4}}{6 \times 10^{-2}} = 1{\cdot}333 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{V}\)

**The three terms.**

\(q_1V_1 = \left(-5 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{6}\right) = -10{\cdot}00\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(q_2V_2 = \left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(1{\cdot}333 \times 10^{6}\right) = +2{\cdot}67\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(U_{\text{mutual}} = -0{\cdot}90\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(\boxed{\ U = -10{\cdot}00 + 2{\cdot}67 - 0{\cdot}90 = -8{\cdot}23\ \mathrm{J}\ }\)

*(The printed scheme states \(-8{\cdot}24\) J, though its own line \(-10 + 2{\cdot}67 - 0{\cdot}90\) gives \(-8{\cdot}23\); the exact value is \(-8{\cdot}2333\) J.)*

**Note that \(r\) means different things in the two halves**, which is the main hazard here. In \(V = A/r\) it is the distance from the **origin** (\(0{\cdot}04\) m and \(0{\cdot}06\) m); in the mutual term it is the distance **between the charges** (\(0{\cdot}1\) m). Using \(0{\cdot}1\) m in the potentials, or the origin distances in the mutual term, is the standard slip.

**Reading the result.** The total is strongly **negative**, dominated by the \(-10\) J that the negative charge gains by sitting in a large positive external potential. The system is bound: \(8{\cdot}23\) J would have to be supplied to dismantle it completely and carry both charges to infinity.
